callouts.label: Unreplicated chromosomes (2n)
callouts.hint: Meiosis I — Interphase. Thin diffuse chromatin threads inside the cell in the Interphase panel (top-left).
callouts.description: During interphase before meiosis, the cell contains 2n chromosomes as diffuse chromatin. DNA replication occurs during S phase, converting each chromosome into two sister chromatids joined at the centromere. By the end of interphase, the cell has 2n chromosomes, each consisting of two identical sister chromatids — the cell is ready to begin meiosis I.
callouts.ap_tip: A common college placement exam mistake: students think meiosis reduces chromosome number from 2n to n during DNA replication. DNA replication DOUBLES the DNA content (2n → 4n DNA) but the chromosome count stays at 2n. The reduction from 2n to n happens during meiosis I when homologs separate.

callouts.label: Synapsis and tetrad formation
callouts.hint: Meiosis I — Prophase I. Paired homologous chromosomes (one pink, one blue) tightly associated in the Prophase I panel (second from left, top row).
callouts.description: During prophase I, homologous chromosomes pair up in a process called synapsis, forming bivalents (tetrads). Each bivalent consists of four chromatids (two sister chromatids from each homolog). The synaptonemal complex holds homologs together, enabling crossing over. This pairing is unique to meiosis — it never occurs in mitosis.
callouts.ap_tip: Synapsis is the KEY event that distinguishes meiosis from mitosis. The college placement exam tests whether students understand that homologs pair in meiosis I but NOT in mitosis. A tetrad = bivalent = 4 chromatids = 2 homologous chromosomes. Know all these terms — the exam uses them interchangeably.

callouts.label: Crossing over (chiasmata)
callouts.hint: Meiosis I — Prophase I. X-shaped contact points between homologs where colors mix (pink-blue) in the Prophase I panel.
callouts.description: Crossing over occurs when non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes exchange segments at points called chiasmata. Enzymes create double-strand breaks in the DNA, and the broken ends are repaired using the homologous chromatid as a template, resulting in recombinant chromosomes with new combinations of maternal and paternal alleles. This is a major source of genetic variation.
callouts.ap_tip: Crossing over produces RECOMBINANT chromosomes — chromosomes with new allele combinations not present in either parent. The college placement exam distinguishes crossing over (exchanges segments between homologs during prophase I) from independent assortment (random orientation of homolog pairs at metaphase I). Both increase genetic diversity but through different mechanisms.

callouts.label: Bivalents at metaphase plate
callouts.hint: Meiosis I — Metaphase I. Paired homologous chromosomes aligned at the center of the cell in the Metaphase I panel (center, top row).
callouts.description: In metaphase I, bivalents (paired homologs) align at the metaphase plate. Each homolog's kinetochore faces a different pole — this is critical because it ensures that homologs (not sister chromatids) will separate in anaphase I. The random orientation of each bivalent (which homolog faces which pole) is the basis of independent assortment.
callouts.ap_tip: Independent assortment occurs HERE at metaphase I. With n bivalents, there are 2^n possible orientations. For humans (n=23), that's 2^23 = 8.4 million possible gamete combinations from independent assortment ALONE — before counting crossing over. This is a classic college placement calculation question.

callouts.label: Independent assortment
callouts.hint: Meiosis I — Metaphase I. The random orientation of homolog pairs at the metaphase plate — each bivalent independently chooses which pole to face.
callouts.description: Independent assortment is the random, independent orientation of each bivalent at the metaphase I plate. For each homologous pair, either the maternal or paternal homolog can face either pole. This random arrangement means that the resulting gametes receive a random mix of maternal and paternal chromosomes, producing genetic variation independent of crossing over.
callouts.ap_tip: Independent assortment follows Mendel's Law of Independent Assortment — genes on different chromosomes sort independently. The college placement exam connects this law to physical chromosome behavior: genes on the SAME chromosome do NOT assort independently (they are linked), which is why crossing over is needed to recombine linked genes.

callouts.label: Homolog separation
callouts.hint: Meiosis I — Anaphase I. Homologous chromosomes (still X-shaped) moving to opposite poles in the Anaphase I panel (fourth, top row).
callouts.description: In anaphase I, homologous chromosomes separate and move to opposite poles. Critically, sister chromatids remain joined at their centromeres — only homologs separate. This is the reductional division that halves the chromosome number from 2n to n. Each pole receives one chromosome from each homologous pair, carrying either the maternal or paternal version (or a recombinant mix after crossing over).
callouts.ap_tip: The college placement exam frequently asks: what separates in anaphase I vs anaphase II? Anaphase I: HOMOLOGS separate (sister chromatids stay together). Anaphase II: SISTER CHROMATIDS separate. This is the single most important distinction between meiosis I and meiosis II.

callouts.label: Sister chromatids still joined
callouts.hint: Meiosis I — Anaphase I. X-shaped chromosomes with centromeres intact — chromatids have NOT separated.
callouts.description: During anaphase I, each chromosome moving to a pole is still composed of two sister chromatids joined at the centromere. Cohesin proteins at the centromere are protected from separase by a protein called shugoshin. Only the cohesin along the chromosome arms is cleaved, allowing homologs to separate while keeping sister chromatids together. The centromeric cohesin will be cleaved later in anaphase II.
callouts.ap_tip: If the college placement exam shows a diagram of anaphase I chromosomes, they should be X-shaped (sister chromatids joined). If they show V-shaped chromosomes, that's anaphase II. This visual distinction is tested in diagram-identification questions.

callouts.label: Two haploid cells (n)
callouts.hint: Meiosis I — Telophase I / Cytokinesis I. Two cells pinching apart in the rightmost panel of the top row.
callouts.description: Telophase I and cytokinesis I produce two haploid cells, each containing n chromosomes (one from each homologous pair). Each chromosome still consists of two sister chromatids. The nuclear envelope may partially reform, and chromosomes may briefly decondense, but these cells proceed quickly into meiosis II without an intervening S phase — there is no DNA replication between meiosis I and meiosis II.
callouts.ap_tip: After meiosis I, each cell is haploid (n) but each chromosome has 2 chromatids, so the DNA content is 2c (not 1c). The college placement exam may ask about DNA content vs. chromosome number at each stage. Meiosis I halves chromosome number (2n→n); meiosis II halves DNA content (2c→1c per cell).

callouts.label: New spindle formation
callouts.hint: Meiosis II — Prophase II. Green spindle fibers forming from orange centrosomes in each cell in the Prophase II panel (leftmost, bottom row).
callouts.description: In prophase II, each haploid cell assembles a new mitotic spindle. Centrosomes duplicate and migrate to opposite poles, and spindle microtubules begin to form. The nuclear envelope (if it reformed) breaks down again. Chromosomes re-condense if they had partially relaxed. This stage is mechanically similar to prophase of mitosis — the key difference is that each cell now contains only n chromosomes.
callouts.ap_tip: Meiosis II is essentially a mitotic division of haploid cells. The college placement exam may ask: how does meiosis II resemble mitosis? Answer: sister chromatids align at the metaphase plate and separate in anaphase — the same events as mitosis. The difference is the starting chromosome number (n vs 2n).

callouts.label: Individual chromatid alignment
callouts.hint: Meiosis II — Metaphase II. X-shaped chromosomes lined up at the metaphase plate in each cell in the Metaphase II panel (second, bottom row).
callouts.description: In metaphase II, individual chromosomes (each still consisting of two sister chromatids) align at the metaphase plate in each cell. Unlike metaphase I, there are no bivalents — each chromosome aligns independently. Kinetochore microtubules from opposite poles attach to the two kinetochores of each chromosome's sister chromatids, preparing for their separation.
callouts.ap_tip: Metaphase II looks like metaphase in mitosis — individual chromosomes at the plate, not paired homologs. The college placement exam tests this: metaphase I has bivalents (tetrads) at the plate; metaphase II has individual chromosomes. The number of chromosomes at the plate in metaphase II is n (half of what you see in mitotic metaphase).

callouts.label: Sister chromatid separation
callouts.hint: Meiosis II — Anaphase II. V-shaped individual chromatids being pulled to opposite poles in each cell in the Anaphase II panel (third, bottom row).
callouts.description: In anaphase II, centromeric cohesin is finally cleaved by separase, allowing sister chromatids to separate. Each chromatid — now an individual chromosome — is pulled to a pole by shortening kinetochore microtubules. The chromatids are V-shaped (not X-shaped) because they are no longer joined. Due to prior crossing over, some of these chromatids carry recombinant combinations of alleles.
callouts.ap_tip: Anaphase II = sister chromatids separate (just like anaphase in mitosis). The V-shape of separating chromatids in anaphase II contrasts with the X-shape of chromosomes in anaphase I. If a nondisjunction error occurs here (chromatids fail to separate), it produces gametes with n+1 and n-1 chromosomes.

callouts.label: Four unique haploid cells
callouts.hint: Meiosis II — Telophase II / Cytokinesis II. Four small cells in a cluster in the rightmost panel of the bottom row.
callouts.description: Meiosis concludes with four genetically unique haploid cells, each containing n chromosomes (one copy of each). These cells are genetically different from each other and from the parent cell due to: (1) crossing over in prophase I, which created recombinant chromosomes, and (2) independent assortment in metaphase I, which randomly distributed maternal and paternal homologs. In males, all four become sperm; in females, typically one becomes an egg and three become polar bodies.
callouts.ap_tip: Meiosis produces 4 GENETICALLY UNIQUE haploid cells. Mitosis produces 2 GENETICALLY IDENTICAL diploid cells. This comparison is the single most tested meiosis concept on the college placement exam. Also know: crossing over + independent assortment + random fertilization = three sources of genetic variation.

callouts.label: Recombinant chromosomes
callouts.hint: Meiosis II — Telophase II / Cytokinesis II. Chromosomes with mixed pink-blue coloring in the final four cells, showing segments exchanged during crossing over.
callouts.description: Recombinant chromosomes carry a mixture of alleles from both parents due to crossing over in prophase I. Each of the four gametes may contain chromosomes with different recombinant configurations. This means that even genes on the same chromosome can be separated into different gametes, increasing genetic diversity beyond what independent assortment alone provides.
callouts.ap_tip: The college placement exam uses recombination frequency to determine how far apart genes are on a chromosome (genetic mapping). Genes far apart on the same chromosome recombine frequently (approaching 50%, appearing unlinked), while genes close together recombine rarely. A recombination frequency of 1% = 1 centimorgan (map unit) of distance.

callouts.label: Nondisjunction risk
callouts.hint: Meiosis I and Meiosis II — Anaphase I or Anaphase II. Nondisjunction can occur at either anaphase when chromosomes fail to separate properly.
callouts.description: Nondisjunction is the failure of chromosomes to separate properly during cell division. In meiosis I, nondisjunction means homologous chromosomes fail to separate, producing gametes with an extra chromosome (n+1) or a missing chromosome (n-1). In meiosis II, nondisjunction means sister chromatids fail to separate. When a gamete with abnormal chromosome number is fertilized, the result is aneuploidy — an abnormal chromosome number in the offspring.
callouts.ap_tip: Nondisjunction causes conditions like Down syndrome (trisomy 21), Turner syndrome (monosomy X), and Klinefelter syndrome (XXY). The college placement exam tests whether nondisjunction occurred in meiosis I or II: if BOTH homologs end up in one gamete, it was meiosis I; if both sister chromatids end up together, it was meiosis II. Draw the diagrams to keep them straight.
